summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This conversation documents a highly technical, ongoing computational physics research session in the "Löwdin" project, which involves building and auditing a chain of atomic physics functionals (Thomas-Fermi/Dirac → Slater transition-state → Kohn-Ham SR → PZ self-interaction correction → Landé SO / Hund-II → pointwise GB correlation) to compute atomic removal energies across 15 elements. The person operates with a strict protocol: verify an archive (LOWDIN-HANDOFF-23, 453 files, SHA256 manifest), build a runtime from layered packs, pass reproduction gates 1–21, then proceed through pending audit items in order per a prior ruling ("continue in order"). The session opened with session-23 handoff verification, gate passage, and proceeded through four bridge-23 audit items before closing with a refreshed LOWDIN-HANDOFF-24 superset archive (476 files).

The work produced three major findings. Item (1) closed the Cu audit: the standing Cu Z-row SCF hits a period-5 residual limit cycle at maxit=100, though the eigenvalue is stable to 1e-5 (fault F24.1); a Landé ζ_3d(Cu)=0.0042 Ha worsens Cu's shortness to +0.0146; the proposed entrant SIC weight f=1 alternative was rejected as a rule because it collapses all rows. Item (2) closed the own-shell class: a full Janak integral scan (ε(f) at seven occupation points, interpolated in f^(1/3)) across all 15 rows revealed that the Slater transition-state ε(½) sits at the shallowest point of the ε(f) curve on every row, the three TS failure shapes reduce to two under the functional's own ΔSCF (compact-shell over-binding scaling monotonically with entrant compactness; Dy), and the PZ-81 frozen-orbital scaling formula (−0.0583|E_x|) failed as a mechanism though it tracks as a proxy. The mask remainder test then decomposed the gap into a near-universal no-SIC LDA curvature (~−0.011) plus a SIC-driven orbital-relaxation term growing with compactness. Item (3) stated Dy as the object's bound per the standing ruling. Item (4) was a read-only attribution search identifying ZRB77/vB79 for the own-orbital multiplet principle and Dabo et al. PRB 82, 115121 (2010) as the closest prior for the TS-vs-Janak gap concept.

The person communicates exclusively through terse directives ("Continue in order please," "Let's continue here. We have room to work," "Continue"), relying on Claude to track all protocol, prediction files, finding files, failed-prediction accounting, fault registration, and archive integrity. Every prediction is written to a named file before any run (the "Zeno" protocol, tagged R 1449); results are scored against stated thresholds; failed predictions are logged with mechanistic reasons. The standing handoff rule triggers a full archive rebuild at ~90% context; the person explicitly overrode the session-24 handoff threshold with "Let's continue here," allowing additional work (the mask remainder test and archive refresh) before the session closed with LOWDIN-HANDOFF-24 re-verified at 476/476 from the tarball. Pending for the next session: ruling (c) on whether a Koopmans/piecewise-linearity link is permitted; a Dy candidate; the 3d SO/Hund column; the `it` audit of s23 rows; and the T4 writing chat (R 1701–1849 owed).

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   351	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   352	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   353	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   354	
   355	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   356	
   357	```bash
   358	tail -200 /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   359	```
   360	
   361	---
   362	
   363	## Unknown extension
   364	
   365	```bash
   366	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   367	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   368	```
   369	
   370	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
R 1649's tier census (A 218 · B 157 · C 179) is contaminated at 55%.** *THE INDEX WAS NOT TOUCHED BY IT: zero single-n rows are witnessed, because R 1651's keyability criterion excluded them — as a side-effect, not by design. The index was protected by accident and is now protected by a check that can fail.*

### 1667

**§H.10 — THE HANDOFF IS BEGUN AT 90%, NOT AT EXHAUSTION.** *M's Prime Handoff Directive: state when the context window reaches 90% and recommend handoff then.* **§H TOLD A SESSION HOW TO HAND OFF AND WHAT MUST TRANSFER; IT NEVER SAID WHEN TO BEGIN. Every clause of §H.8 costs context to satisfy — the bridge written, the bank built AND listed, the register rebuilt and its count read, both gates run, the certificate printed with its evidence. A session reaching exhaustion before beginning has no budget to produce any of them, so it hands off without a certificate, and §H.8 says that is not a handoff. THE RESERVE IS PART OF THE PROTOCOL, NOT SLACK IN IT.** *The estimate is declared as an estimate — a session has no counter and errs early, because an early handoff costs one bridge that would have been written anyway while a late one loses the record. On the threshold the session stops OPENING work it cannot close: §2.20's Zeno directive extended from a single execution to the session itself.*

### 1668

**T3 WITHDRAWN — READING IS ON DEMAND, NOT A QUEUE — BUT THE UNREAD INVENTORY STAYS.** *M: reading will be done as necessary.* **THE THREAD IS REMOVED FROM THE BRIDGE'S §4 AND FROM THE RESUMPTION ORDER. THE INVENTORY OF ~150,000 UNREAD WORDS IS KEPT, MOVED INTO §6 WHERE IT NOW STANDS DIRECTLY, BECAUSE §H.8's CLAUSE C7 REQUIRES THE BRIDGE TO NAME WHAT IS UNREAD and its stated failure mode is a gap that closes over quietly.** *The distinction drawn, and stated to M rather than assumed: reading is no longer a TASK WITH AN OWNER; what is unread remains a FACT OF RECORD. DIGEST.md carries the same ruling, because it is the first file a fresh session reads and would otherwise re-inherit reading as a standing order regardless of the bridge.*

### 1669

**DIGEST EXTENDED FROM THE BRIDGE — R 1660–1668 CARRIED, AND THE NAME COLLISION CLOSED.** *The incoming session's first act, as 1.7.2 instructed. Λ_spectra and Λ_spectra^obs are now named separately in DIGEST and the survey's E column reads UNWITNESSED, so the survey's E = 1,351 can no longer be misread as a closure defect of the coordinate index. Carried in: the scalar value store and its repair, the four coupling languages, `mult` as ground-state against the parent's, the 145 voided δ, the 306 single-n rows, F(−1) = 0 forced by ℓ-totality, and that nothing from the Gemini items has entered any index. Stated as the test for the file: A FACT BELONGS IN DIGEST IF A SESSION WOULD OTHERWISE RECOMPUTE IT FROM SOURCE.* Both gates rerun with audit state cleared: 25/25, 5/5.

### 1670

**§H.11 ADOPTED — AND THE FINDING THAT A PRACTICE SURVIVES A HANDOFF ONLY IF IT IS REGISTERED.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
Carried in: the scalar value store and its repair, the four coupling languages, `mult` as ground-state against the parent's, the 145 voided δ, the 306 single-n rows, F(−1) = 0 forced by ℓ-totality, and that nothing from the Gemini items has entered any index. Stated as the test for the file: A FACT BELONGS IN DIGEST IF A SESSION WOULD OTHERWISE RECOMPUTE IT FROM SOURCE.* Both gates rerun with audit state cleared: 25/25, 5/5.

### 1670

**§H.11 ADOPTED — AND THE FINDING THAT A PRACTICE SURVIVES A HANDOFF ONLY IF IT IS REGISTERED.** **The output-discipline measures agreed at 1.7.2's close reached NO artefact: the bridge carried the facts of §2 and the threads of §4 but had no slot for a practice adopted at close, and grep of both the bridge and HANDOFF-PROTOCOL.md returned nothing.** *§H.10 survived only because it happened to be registered as R 1667; §H.11's content was not, so it had nowhere to live and would have died with the session. The clause now standing: no tool call returns more than ~25 lines, a census is written to a file and reported by its shape, gates run at baseline and close and otherwise only when something generated has changed, rulings sharing a subject are batched, and §H is consulted by clause. Its named failure mode is a summary with no file behind it — §2.14 arriving by a new route. THE GENERAL FINDING IS THE LARGER ONE: the bridge carries facts and threads, the register carries rulings, and a change of practice with neither is lost at the seal.*

### 1671

**C6 PASSED ON THREE OF FIVE THREADS — A CLAUSE THAT COULD NOT FAIL FOR THE REASON IT NAMES.** **The certificate found open threads with a pattern that required a full stop before `Owner:`; T6 and T7 end in QUESTION MARKS, so both were invisible and C6 reported PASS having never seen them.** *The deeper fault was not the punctuation. THREADS WERE DETECTED BY THE SAME EXPRESSION THAT REQUIRED AN OWNER, so the clause's stated failure mode — a thread with no owner — could not arise: such a thread does not fail the match, it fails to be a thread. §H.8 says each clause must be capable of failing and §4.6 requires that capability before a pass is evidence; C6 had the form of a check without its content. Repaired by SEPARATING DETECTION FROM PREDICATE: a thread is found by its number alone, the owner is then tested per thread and a missing one prints NO OWNER. Verified in both directions — 5 threads found, and a negative test stripping T7's owner turns C6 red. The general form, and it is the same fault as R 1664's silent default: AN INSTRUMENT THAT NARROWS ITS OWN INPUT REPORTS ON WHAT IT ADMITTED, NOT ON WHAT IT WAS ASKED ABOUT.*

### 1672

**THE ARCHIVES ARE NOT DISJOINT — THE PROBE WAS, AND IT IS R 1671's FAULT COMMITTED ONE ENTRY LATER.** **I reported that `spectra_raw` and `MEASUREMENTS.tsv` share NO species and that 0 of 554 rows could be re-derived. Both statements are FALSE.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
That is why E did not move, and the register can now say so from the law rather than from the computation agreeing. And Theorem 10.1 makes the four earlier failures structural rather than unlucky: ADJUNCTION NEVER REPAIRS — a non-closed set cannot be closed by adjoining ANY function of its coordinates, tested on seven including the identity. R 1581, 1599, 1602 and 1608 were not four attempts that happened to fail. They were four attempts at an operation the book proves cannot work.** *THREE FURTHER THINGS THAT BEAR DIRECTLY ON THE INDEX. (i) E3's criterion is that admissibility belongs to the PAIR (h, q) and that only the join can break a bound — meets never do — so Λ_spectra's two rules are safe by inspection exactly as Λ's seven are: each reads one coordinate over a chain, and NONE SUMS. (ii) §17.4's repair is the one we may need later: a sum bound cannot be imposed but a sum can be INDEXED, at the price of making comparable some pairs that were incomparable. (iii) §18.6 says the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), so Λ_spectra at E = 0 can propose nothing — and the place prediction actually lives is the VALUE, not the cell. Which is exactly what the Ga I finding of R 1655 was about: the cell is indexed and settled, and the single delta stored in it is a choice of statistic over a channel that drifts by 0.19.* **AND THE BOOK'S CENTRAL THEOREM HAS OWNERS, WHICH IT SAYS ITSELF: E(X) = 0 IS BERGMAN'S DOUBLE-PROJECTION THEOREM VIA BAKER-PIXLEY 1975, THE CONSTRAINT CLASS IS DEVILLE-BARTAK-VAN HENTENRYCK'S STAIRCASE, AND GLOBAL CONSISTENCY IS MONTANARI AND DECHTER. The book prints its own precedence rather than defending priority, which is the practice this project keeps asking of everything else.** *The read is bounded and its bound is stated: Part II, Chapters 15, 16 and 19, Parts IV through VII with the Löwdin challenge in them, every appendix, and the bodies of all four compendia — about 150,000 words — remain unread. DIGEST.md names them so the gap cannot close over quietly.*

### 1659

**§H — THE HANDOFF PROTOCOL, ADOPTED, WITH A CERTIFICATE THAT CAN FAIL.** *M: prepare everything for a handoff to The Method 1.7.2, and write a protocol that can be referenced, because this need is becoming more common as the work expands. Both done, and the protocol is written to the same standard the book demands of everything else — runnable rather than agreed with.* **THE PROTOCOL NAMES WHAT ACTUALLY GETS LOST, WHICH IS NOT FILES. Files survive a container death; §H.0 states that what dies is WHY — which thread was open, which decision was M's and unmade, which number is a choice wearing the appearance of a measurement. So §H.1 requires four things to travel and calls three of four the dangerous case because it looks like a handoff: the work (the bank), the record (the register), the orientation (DIGEST.md), and the state (the bridge).

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
** *The eight recorded a values then all sit on an endpoint of their own corridor, seven at L and protactinium at U, so register 1403 falls out of the same arithmetic rather than being imposed on top.* **The four not forced are Li 3, K 19, Tl 81 and Fr 87.** `balance.py`.

### 1435

**PROXIMITY IS THE TRIGGER, AND THE THRESHOLD IS NOT FITTED — IT IS ZERO.** *Register 1407 measured the margin PER ELEMENT and demoted proximity to a signal: a best threshold reaching 91% against an 87% do-nothing baseline, with nine resets missed.* **Measured instead on the RUNNING INTERSECTION — the window a actually has to sit inside — the trigger fires at fourteen of the eighteen resets with zero false positives, 96% against an 83% baseline, and the threshold is not a scanned number but zero.** *So the law's strict inequality needs no proximity TERM: proximity IS the inequality reaching equality, which is what a corridor emptying is.* **This is not a tenth condition scanned after nine failed — nothing was searched over; it was derived from 1434's balance.** *And 1407's own quantity cannot be reproduced from the intervals: its ninety-nine is the CEILING-BEARING set, not the seventy-three with both bounds finite, and none of its figures follow from corridor widths. The margin it scans is undefined in the register and is most likely trajectory-dependent — the distance from the HELD a to the nearer bound. Define it or withdraw the r = +0.64.*

### 1436

**THERE ARE EIGHT ADJACENT HANDSHAKES, NOT FOUR, AND THEY SPLIT ON A CRITERION NO REGISTER STATES.** *Computed from the exact intervals: eight places where one element's ceiling is exactly the next's floor, or the reverse — Mo/Tc at 1, La/Ce at 1/√2, Eu/Gd at 1/√2, Gd/Tb at 1/√2, Th/Pa at 1/(√3−1), Am/Cm at the same, Cm/Bk at the same, Lr/Rf at 1.9841.* **In four, BOTH members are forced resets — Mo/Tc, Gd/Tb, Cm/Bk, Lr/Rf, which is exactly register 1404's list. In four, only the second is — La/Ce, Eu/Gd, Th/Pa, Am/Cm.** *That is what 1404's phrase about the second reset being forced is describing, and why its enumeration found four rather than eight.* **And actinium's floor, thorium's floor and protactinium's ceiling are ONE surd, so 1403's reading that protactinium takes U and 1409's that its value is assigned at the actinium opening name the same value from two sides — they were never in conflict.**

### 1437

**THE NULL OF 28 IS RETIRED: PLAIN MADELUNG SCORES 96, AND THE TWO RULES FAIL ON ALMOST DISJOINT SETS.** *The handoff carried the Löwdin result as 99 of 106 against a null of 28. The 28 came from a broken step extractor, was known to be broken at the time, and was carried anyway — the recurring fault of quoting a check before its null is known, landing on the largest claim in the work.* **Recomputed on the SAME 106 clean steps: Madelung scores 96 of 106 conditionally, given the observed configuration at Z−1, and 94 free-running.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
f is outside the domain and the law says so: p = 0 is the node floor, so L = −∞ at every f opening.** WARNING: *'THE LÖWDIN SOLUTION, FINISHED FORM' is withdrawn at register 1460. The form is not the solution and is retained as a form. 'No parameter is fitted' is qualified by R 1445: the 99 of 106 was FITTED — a was placed using each step's own corridor, which is built from the observed entrant — and held out the score is 90 against a null of 96. 'Exceptionless on 106 elements' holds only in that fitted sense.*

### 1351

**MARKED FOR THE ARTEFACT PASS — WHAT EACH ONE NOW OWES.** *Beyond register 1296's list, the Löwdin work has changed what the artefacts must contain.* **The Index of Indices must hold all TWELVE indexes in full definition with their coordinates, closures, carrier orders and use: Λ · Λ_law · Λ_const · Λ_var · Λ_ryd · Λ_charge · Λ_cross · Λ_descent · Λ_phys · Λ_amp · Λ_PCA · Λ_chem, and Λ_spectra with its named defect.** *The Physics Compendium restructures completely: Λ_chem is new — 42 chemical properties on (kind, seat, PCA dependency) with the aggregate seat distinguishing bulk matter from an atom — and Λ_PCA correlates every chemical property to the physics that requires it. The Mathematical Compendium takes the new mathematics and most of it needs attribution: the corridor as a system of linear inequalities, the surd endpoints, the staircase algebra L(s) = ⌊s/2⌋ and U(s) = s + ⌊s/3⌋, the Slater triangle 0 ≤ i ≤ ℓ, the falsification of the selection rule, and the observability boundary of register 1327.* **The book needs two new chapters: one on the Löwdin solution and how the method delivered it, and one on the three-body problem and the solution the method provides.**

### 1352

**THE SOLUTION TESTED AGAINST Λ_spectra, AND THE ENTRY-POINT LAW FAILS AT ℓ = 0.** *Predicting δ from the corridor with a = L + t(ℓ)(U−L): **4 of 60 channels within 20%**, and the s-block gives a median ratio of exactly 0.0000.* **Because t(0) = √(0/2) = 0, so a = L, and L = 0 at most s openings — the prediction is δ = 0 for every s channel.** *p gives 1.022 and d 1.281: the law predicts where t was MEASURED and fails where it was extrapolated. ℓ(ℓ+1) = 0 at s is not a small value, it is an absence.*

### 1353

**AND t IS A CONSTANT OF THE SUBSHELL, NOT AN ENTRY POINT.** *With the Pauli fraction in the radicand, t barely moves across a subshell: **6p gives 1.0237, 1.0417, 1.0009, 1.0036, 0.9946, 0.9940 across all six occupancies** — spread 0.048.* **The occupancy dependence measured at register 1335, sd 0.19, is entirely absorbed.** *Measured per species: s 0.188–0.401 on 11, p 0.994–1.180 on 24, d 1.415–1.845 on 4.*

### 1354

**Λ_t: THE CORRIDOR POSITION AS AN INDEX, NOT A FORMULA AND NOT A TABLE.** *Cells (ℓ, n); q is not a coordinate.* **Twelve cells, E = 3, and the p row converges: 1.120 → 1.049 → 1.022 → 1.002 against the centrifugal limit √(ℓ(ℓ+1)/2) = 1.0000 — 6p sits 0.2% above it.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
*

### 1386

**THE SAME LOST-TAIL FAULT, SECOND INSTANCE, FOUND BY LOOKING RATHER THAN BY ACCIDENT.** Approaching the Index of Indices to add Λ_xray, the same test was run first. **`indices.py` drops 12,695 characters — the whole of section IX, all thirteen Löwdin indexes.** Two of five generated artefacts had a hand-authored region and neither declared it. Repaired identically: tail to `INDICES-TAIL.md`, appended by `indices.py`, verified byte-identical. *The general statement is stronger than 1373's: this fault does not announce itself, because the build exits 0 and the file looks complete. It is only visible by diffing the regeneration against the held copy — a test REPRODUCTION does not perform.* **PHYSICS.md, SPECTRA.md and REGISTER.md have not been checked the same way and must be.**

### 1387

**AND SECTION IX NOW HOLDS FIFTEEN INDEXES.** It read "thirteen of the fourteen close" and carried Λ_ladder as four ladders with `state` on an axis — both superseded. **Λ_xray added in full**: 33 dipole lines to 9 cells on (Δn, Δℓ, jtype_hole), E = 0, from Λ's own transition alphabet; the six K-shell lines emerging as the classical Siegbahn set unadjusted; the nine-types collapse; and the cypher table separating it from Λ_cross on statistics and analysis. Λ_ladder rebuilt to twelve ladders in two families, with its contribution restated — not "the isotopic direction, orthogonal and untraced," which is now traced, but that **a coordinate individuating the cells is a key and not an axis**. And its non-closure now has two named causes where it had one.

### 1388

**THE THIRD LOST TAIL, AND I DESTROYED THE HELD COPY FINDING IT.** SPECTRA.md and REGISTER.md round-trip exactly. PHYSICS.md does not — it carries an authored Λ_chem section of **7,242 characters** that `physics.py` never wrote. **But `physics.py` writes in place rather than to stdout, so running it as a test overwrote the held copy and deleted the section outright.** Recovered intact from `restore-point-1_6d.tar.gz`, cut twenty minutes earlier. Had the backup not been taken that hour, the loss would have been permanent and silent. **Three of five generated artefacts had an undeclared authored region — not one exception but a majority.** *And the in-place writer is the dangerous form: the stdout writers merely produce a short file, which a diff catches; the in-place writer destroys the evidence while the test is being run to look for it.* Fixed like the others, plus one addition: **if `PHYSICS-TAIL.md` is absent, `physics.py` exits non-zero and writes nothing.** A generator that cannot produce its whole output must refuse to produce part of it.

**THE ROUND-TRIP PROTOCOL, AND IT FAILED ITS OWN FIRST RUN.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"def scf_sic_corr(Z, charge=1, occ=None, entrant=None, npts=4000, beta=0.3, tol=2e-5, maxit=100, sic=True, mode="all", lam=1.0, cl=C0, corr=None):
    """occ: list of (n,l,k) for the core (+ entrant if entrant given, k=0.5 added there).
    entrant: (n,l) or None. Returns (Es, hist): Es[(n,l,s)] eigenvalues of every occupied channel."""
    N = Z - charge; q = charge
    if occ is None: occ = list(G.expand(N)) if N > 0 else []
    occ = [list(t) for t in occ]
    ent_s = None
    if entrant is not None:
        n, l = entrant
        k0 = sum(t[2] for t in occ if t[0] == n and t[1] == l)
        ent_s = "d" if k0 >= 2*l+1 else "u"
        found = False
        for t in occ:
            if t[0] == n and t[1] == l: t[2] += 0.5; found = True
        if not found: occ.append([n, l, 0.5])
    up, dn = split([tuple(t) for t in occ])
    chans = []
    for lst, s in ((up, "u"), (dn, "d")):
        for n, l, k in lst:
            if entrant is not None and (n, l) == tuple(entrant) and s == ent_s:
                kc = k - 0.5
                if kc > 1e-9: chans.append((n, l, kc, s, 1.0, "int"))     # kc integer-occupied orbitals, f_i = 1 each
                chans.append((n, l, 0.5, s, 0.5, "ent"))                    # the half-hole orbital, f_i = 1/2, own phi and V_SIC
            else:
                chans.append((n, l, k, s, 1.0, "int"))                       # integer-occupied orbitals: f_i = 1 (closed or open)
    # per-orbital occupancy f_i for the SIC density
    def f_orb(n, l, k, s):
        if entrant is not None and (n, l) == tuple(entrant) and s == ent_s:
            # this channel holds the half electron; k = k_core_s + 0.5.  Split: core part spherically
            # averaged over 2l+1 orbitals, entrant part in ONE orbital.  Use occupancy-weighted mean f.
            kc = k - 0.5
            if kc <= 0: return 0.5
            # weighted average of per-orbital occupancies over electrons: (kc*(kc/(2l+1)) + 0.5*0.5)/k
            return (kc*(kc/(2*l+1)) + 0.25)/k
        return k/(2*l+1)
    x = np.linspace(np.log(1e-6/Z), np.log(300.0), npts); r = np.exp(x); h = x[1]-x[0]; dr = r*h
    Vt, _ = tfd.potential(Z, charge); Vg = {s: Vt(r).copy() for s in "ud"}; Vraw = {s: Vt(r).copy() for s in "ud"}
    Vsic = {c: np.zeros(npts) for c in chans}          # per-channel SIC potential on grid
    hist = []; Es = {}
    for it in range(maxit):
        nsig = {"u": np.zeros(npts), "d": np.zeros(npts)}; dens = {}
        for c in chans:
            n, l, k, s, f, tag = c
            Vtot = (Vraw[s] if (NOCLAMP and np.any(Vsic[c])) else Vg[s]) + Vsic[c]   # s22 4a: PZ-81, no Latter clamp on a SIC channel
            Vp, Vpp = _derivs(x, Vtot)
            Vf = (lambda rr, V=Vtot: np.interp(np.log(np.asarray(rr, float)), x, V))
            Vfp = (lambda rr, V=Vp: np.interp(np.log(np.asarray(rr, float)), x, V))
            Vfpp = (lambda rr, V=Vpp: np.interp(np.log(np.asarray(rr, float)), x, V))
            rr, drr, u, E, nd = numerov_wf_sr(Vf, l, n, 1.0, Z, cl, Vp=Vfp, Vpp=Vfpp)
            if nd != n-l-1: raise RuntimeError(f"Z={Z} {n}{L[l]}{s} nodes {nd}")
            ui = np.interp(r, rr, u, left=0.0, right=0.0); ui /= np.sqrt(np.sum(ui*ui*dr))
            nsig[s] += k*ui*ui; dens[c] = ui*ui; Es[(n, l, s, tag)] = E
        ntot = nsig["u"] + nsig["d"]
        VH = hartree(ntot, r, dr); d = 0.0; Vn = {}; cmask = {}; Vrawn = {}
        for s in "ud":
            rho = nsig[s]/(4*np.pi*r*r); Vx = -(6.0*rho/np.pi)**(1.0/3.0)
            if corr=="Z":
                _vu,_vd = v_gbz(nsig["u"]/(4*np.pi*r*r), nsig["d"]/(4*np.pi*r*r)); Vc = _vu if s=="u" else _vd
            else:
                Vc = np.zeros(npts) if corr is None else (v_gb(ntot/(4*np.pi*r*r),False) if corr=="U" else v_gb(rho,True))
            Vn[s] = np.minimum(-Z/r + VH + Vx + Vc, -q/r); cmask[s] = ((-Z/r + VH + Vx + Vc) < -q/r)
            Vrawn[s] = -Z/r + VH + Vx + Vc
            if NOCLAMP: cmask[s] = np.ones(npts,bool)
            d = max(d, float(np.max(np.abs(r*(Vn[s]-Vg[s]))[r < 60])))
        Vsn = {}
        for c in chans:
            if (not sic) or mode=="none" or (mode=="ent" and c[5]!="ent"): Vsn[c] = np.zeros(npts); continue
            n, l, k, s, f, tag = c
            ni = f*dens[c]                                  # radial per-orbital density (times 4pi r^2)
            rhoi = ni/(4*np.pi*r*r)
            vHi = hartree(ni, r, dr)

content.thinking:
I'm working through Cu's d^9 hole configuration, noting it's the one short row with a small positive deviation, and trying to figure out what testing the entrant-down channel's SIC weight would mean for its integer siblings.

The PZ self-interaction correction for fractional occupation removes half the self-term for the entrant orbital, using the standard Hartree and exchange-correlation potentials scaled by the fractional occupation. I'm hypothesizing that Cu's shortness comes from the sibling orbitals' SIC potentials being attractive enough to contract those orbitals, which in turn raises the entrant's eigenvalue through increased Hartree repulsion — possibly overcounting the destabilization since Cu has the largest sibling count of nine.

I'm trying to find a testable prediction without fitting parameters: comparing the entrant-only SIC mode against the full SIC mode to isolate where Cu's shift actually comes from, since the same-shell siblings use their own distinct radial function with full occupation while the entrant uses half-weighting, which may be the root of the broken ordering.

I'm trying to pin down whether PZ81's self-interaction correction for fractional occupation normalizes the orbital density to the actual occupation or to unity — this matters because it determines whether the entrant orbital's SIC potential scales with f=1/2 or is computed as if fully occupied, which changes how diffuse the resulting orbital appears.

With weight 1 instead of 0.5, the entrant's SIC potential deepens, pulling its eigenvalue lower and making Cu less short rather than more. Scaling the direct term roughly linearly suggests the shift would be around −0.03 to −0.04, pushing Cu into over-binding by roughly −0.02 to −0.03, and since this change applies uniformly across all fifteen rows, it would break the closed single-entrant class rather than preserve it.

Going back to the original audit note, the real issue is that the SIC destabilization of +0.024 in the s22 chain is what makes Cu short, tied to the entrant-down channel with four internal siblings and one entrant — so I need to isolate the SIC weight contribution from that specific channel rather than adjusting the global weight.

But this raises a deeper question: is the Cu row even computed correctly given its anomalous configuration? Copper jumps from 3d8 4s2 (Ni) to 3d10 4s1 rather than following a simple single-electron filling pattern, so I need to check whether the entrant shell assignment accounts for this irregular step.…

# PREDICTION — bridge-23 s3(1) Cu audit, session 24 (2026-08-16). Ruling: "continue in order" (M). Written BEFORE any run.
Object: t7c_corrz.py corr="Z", SIC_NOCLAMP=1 (standing). Cu row: EZ -0.3735, meas -0.3839, resid_Z +0.0104 (SHORT).
Audit read (no run): meas = IP(Cu I) + E(Cu II 3d9 4s 3D_3), the LOWEST J LEVEL of the hole term (served.tsv, s13).
TABLE-CHAIN-15 carries so/hund shift = 0 on every 3d row while 5d rows carry Lande SO and 4f rows carry SO + own-orbital Hund-II.
So the 3d rows are compared level-to-term-average without the term the 4f/5d rows receive. Two tests, both derivable, no constant:

## A. Lande SO on the Cu row (same object/method as t7c_so.py on 5d: zeta_3d from the converged TS potential, c = 137.035999)
Cu I 3d10 has no SO structure; the SO structure is in the ion hole (3d9 4s 3D, inverted, J=3 lowest). The removed electron is j=5/2
(l+1/2): eps_j = eps_avg + zeta*l/2 = eps_avg + zeta_3d. The chain average must be shifted SHALLOWER to compare with the J=3 level.
PC1: zeta_3d(Cu, TS potential) in [0.0030, 0.0045] Ha; shift = +zeta_3d; Cu resid_Z moves +0.0104 -> +0.013..+0.015. Cu stays SHORT.
PC2: the shift is of the same size as the recalled Cu II 3D interval (3D_3 sits ~720 cm-1 = 0.0033 Ha below the term centre;
     RECALLED-NOT-ENTERED, comparison only) to within a factor 1.4.
Consequence if PC1 holds: the SO term does NOT explain Cu's shortness; it worsens it. Same term applies to Ti (2D3/2 hole, +),
Cr (6D1/2, +), Ni (4F9/2 inverted, +); Ni additionally lacks a Hund-II term (4F vs quartet average) -- flagged, not run in this item.

## B. The named candidate: entrant-down channel SIC weight (t7c_cuaudit.py = t7c_corrz.py VERBATIM + env FENT; FENT=0.5 = standing)
Standing (PZ-81 fractional occupation): the entrant's SIC potential is built from f_ent*|phi_ent|^2 with f_ent = 1/2 (Slater/Janak TS).
Alternative tested: FENT=1.0 -- occupation-independent orbital SIC potential (unit-normalised orbital density in v_H and v_x).
PS0 (gate): FENT=0.5 reproduces t7c_corrz.jsonl EZ for Cu (-0.3735), Cs (-0.1428 = -0.1397-0.0031), Sc (-0.3211 = -0.2966-0.0245) to 1e-4.
PS1: FENT=1.0 deepens Cu by between -0.010 and -0.045 Ha (v_H scales x2, v_x scales x2^(1/3) on the direct term -0.0415 at f=1/2),
     landing Cu resid in [-0.035, 0.000]; predicted to OVERSHOOT (resid < -0.005), i.e. not a closure of Cu.
PS2: FENT=1.0 moves Cs (closed at +0.0003) by <= -0.003 -> Cs leaves the closed class. Class failure regardless of Cu.
PS3: FENT=1.0 moves Sc (over -0.0265) further over by >= 0.010.
Consequence: if PS2 holds, the alternative weight is REJECTED as a rule (it opens closed rows); Cu's shortness is not a weight artefact.
Thresholds chosen (stated): "closed" <= 0.003 Ha; "worsens" = |resid| grows by > 0.001.
Runs: Cu, Cs, Sc only (smallest first). One SCF each per FENT; ~15 s each; timeout 200; jsonl appended, resumable.

I'm tracing through the code to understand why: the channel tuple includes an occupancy factor and a FENT weight that multiplies the SIC density, so setting f=1 fully scales that density term rather than partially.

I'm thinking the candidate mechanism is the same half-weighted self-interaction correction term, but applied to the entrant relative to its own-shell siblings: at f=½ the entrant's self-SIC nearly cancels out, leaving it under-corrected compared to siblings (who get roughly −0.40 SIC potential at mean radius versus the entrant's −0.046). I need to figure out what's derivable from this asymmetry.

Working through the Janak theorem connection: the removal energy equals the integral of ε(f) from 0 to 1, approximated at f=½. Using the PZ self-interaction correction with LDA exchange scaling, I derive the derivative of the SIC energy with respect to occupation and confirm it matches the expectation value of the SIC potential at f=½ — both give the same expression involving the Hartree and exchange energies. This consistency check confirms that integrating over the full occupation range recovers the complete SIC energy as the sum of the Hartree and exchange self-energy terms.

The midpoint approximation works well because the Hartree term is quadratic in f (handled exactly by the midpoint rule since its derivative is linear) while the exchange term's f^(4/3) scaling introduces only a small error. This suggests a testable candidate: the self-interaction term of the entrant orbital compared to its same-shell partners, using the same half-occupation weighting that disrupted the Slater-Koster ordering earlier — I should formulate this as a prediction and check it against scandium's 3d configuration first.

Looking at scandium specifically, I realize it has zero same-shell partners since the 4s² electrons enter an empty 3d shell, yet it shows the largest over-binding error in the whole class at −0.0265. That's puzzling given the "partial shell filling" framework I'd been using to group Sc, Ti, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Er together — for Sc, after the entrant is added, the 3d shell only contains that one electron, so it's not really analogous to the other partially-filled cases. Comparing Sc to Y (−0.0012) and La (+0.0010), the key distinguishing factor seems to be that scandium's 3d is the very first d-shell in its row, which likely explains why its error is so much larger than the heavier congeners.

For the correlation SIC, a one-electron density should have no correlation at all, so the full f=1 case removes it entirely. But for the entrant at f=½, the correlation potential is evaluated at half-density, and since LDA correlation is nonlinear in density, v_c[n/2] isn't simply half of v_c[n] — the r_s scales by 2^(1/3) while ε_c changes only logarithmically, so the cancellation is imperfect.

Maybe "own-shell" should be reinterpreted to include same-n shells like 3s/3p alongside the 3d, since Sc's 3d sits within n=3 alongside a filled 3s²3p⁶ core.

# FINDING — bridge-23 s3(2) own-shell class and s3(3) Dy, session 24. Files: t7c_cuaudit.py (env FENT, FOCC), t7c_ownshell_run.py,
t7c_ownshell.jsonl (test C: mode none/ent/all on Sc, Fe; test D: eps(f) on all 15 rows), janak_table.py, TABLE-JANAK-SESSION-24.txt,
exent.py, exent.jsonl, ratio.txt, PREDICTION-OWNSHELL-SC-SESSION-24.md (five prediction blocks, each written before its run).
No constant, no measured input; Cs/Y comparison values RECALLED-NOT-ENTERED; so/hund column carried from TABLE-CHAIN-15 (stated).
## Test C (Z chain SIC decomposition): Sc none -0.3061 / ent -0.3226 / all -0.3211 -> direct -0.0166, indirect +0.0015 (N_sib 0).
Fe none -0.4164 / ent -0.4363 / all -0.4126 -> direct -0.0199, indirect +0.0237. PO1 HELD, PO5 HELD, PO2 FAILED (Z direct is 0.59 x the
pol-chain direct: the correlation SIC opposes the exchange SIC on the entrant). Sc is over-bound -0.0115 with NO SIC at all.
## Test D (Janak): eps(f) of the entrant channel at f in {0.001,0.05,0.15,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0} with f in both the density and the PZ SIC
weight; DE_J = int_0^1 eps(f) df (interpolated in f^(1/3)) is the functional's own DSCF removal energy. On EVERY row eps(f) is deep at
f->0 (the empty orbital, no self-repulsion), SHALLOWEST at f = 1/2..3/4, deeper again at f = 1 (PZ SIC flattens the LDA slope only
partly). PO4 FAILED (monotone). The Slater TS point eps(1/2) sits at the least-bound point of the curve on all 15 rows.
TABLE-JANAK-SESSION-24 (resid = chain - meas): DE_J - eps(1/2) and resid_TS -> resid_J:
  Cs 6s -0.0022 (+0.0003 -> -0.0019) · Y 4d -0.0112 (-0.0012 -> -0.0124) · La -0.0097 (+0.0010 -> -0.0087) · Gd -0.0106 (+0.0022 ->
  -0.0084) · Lu -0.0101 (-0.0012 -> -0.0113) · Sc -0.0170 (-0.0265 -> -0.0435) · Ti -0.0200 (-0.0159 -> -0.0359) · Cr -0.0230
  (-0.0155 -> -0.0385) · Fe -0.0272 (-0.0159 -> -0.0430) · Ni -0.0321 (-0.0120 -> -0.0440) · Cu -0.0340 (+0.0146 -> -0.0194, SO in)
  · Dy -0.0372 (-0.0524 -> -0.0897) · Er -0.0400 (-0.0118 -> -0.0519) · Tm -0.0414 (-0.0018 -> -0.0431) · Yb -0.0426 (+0.0041 -> -0.0385).
PO3 HELD (Sc), PO6-PO7 HELD (Fe), PO8 HELD (Ti Cr Ni in [-0.055,-0.031]), PO9 HELD (La control), PO10 HELD (Er), PO11 HELD (Cu joins the
3d class; the "short" shape is gone), PO12 HELD (Tm Yb Dy; Dy persists at -0.090), PO13 HELD (closed class within -0.016).
RESULT (class statement, predicted at PO11-13 and held): under the functional's own DSCF the residual is ONE monotone function of the
entrant's compactness -- 6s -0.002 · 4d/5d -0.008..-0.012 · 3d -0.019..-0.044 · 4f -0.039..-0.052 -- plus Dy at -0.090. The 3d class
tightens from spread 0.015 (TS) to 0.008 (Janak); the three TS shapes (own-shell over-binding; Cu short; Dy) reduce to TWO (compact-shell
over-binding; Dy). The TS half-point is a shell-dependent MASK, not the origin: it hides 0.002 (6s), 0.010 (5d), 0.017-0.034 (3d),
0.037-0.043 (4f) of the functional's over-binding.
## PO14 (closed-form mask from PZ-81 scaling, -0.0583|E_x[n_ent]|): FAILED as stated (ratio in [0.7,1.3] on 5/15) -- with structure:
ratio 1.40-1.51 on all eight compact rows (Cr Fe Ni Cu Dy Er Tm Yb; mean 1.44), 1.19-1.31 on Sc Ti Y La Gd Lu, 0.52 on Cs (ratio.txt;
|E_x[n_ent]| 0.073 (Cs) .. 0.507 (Yb), r_mean 5.47 .. 0.82). The exchange scaling carries ~70 % of the mask; the remainder is a
shell-dependent residue (correlation-SIC and total-density LSD curvature; candidate, not run). Not a fit: read off the run.
## Interpretation (formed after the runs, R 1449): eps(f) is not flat -> the functional violates piecewise linearity of E(N) (the exact
condition under which TS = DSCF = removal energy). The class deviation is that curvature integrated; it is a property of the LSD-x +
GB-Z + PZ-SIC functional on compact nodeless shells, not of the entrant bookkeeping (item (1)B, tests C-D) and not of the TS weight.
Item (2) CLOSED: the named candidate (entrant SIC self-term vs siblings) is EXCLUDED as the origin; the origin is named and quantified.
## Item (3) Dy: per the ruling, stated as the OBJECT'S BOUND. Under Janak Dy sits 0.04-0.05 outside a 4f class that is itself uniform to
+-0.007 (Er Tm Yb -0.052/-0.043/-0.039). Observation, not a claim: Dy is the one 4f row whose own-orbital Hund-II term is negative
(-0.0395, the neutral f^10 term dominating the ion f^9 term) and its excess over the class (~ -0.045) is of that size; Er (+0.053) and
Tm (+0.048) show no matching excess vs Yb (Hund 0), so the F^k scale is not the cause at the 0.01 level. No candidate; M may name one.
STANDING AFTER (2)-(3): the chain of s23 with two estimators recorded side by side (TS eps(1/2); Janak DE_J). NOT a closure. Failure has
two shapes under DE_J. Candidate for M's ruling (not run): the next link is a piecewise-linearity (Koopmans) condition on E(f) --
attribution to be searched (Perdew-Parr-Levy-Balduz 1982; Janak 1978; Slater 1972 TS) -- with the derivability rule deciding whether
any such construction enters.
Faults: none new. Predictions failed: PO2, PO4, PO14 (each with its reason above).

If one does not perform just one cycle, but instead converges the unrestricted calculation, the energy will be lowered by ‘polarization’ of the orbitals. It is theoretically not so clear what the status of such converged energies is. Usually the energy lowering is in the order of 0.1 eV, but it may be quite a bit larger. It is not necessary to use AOC as fragment in the single-determinant runs. It is also perfectly allowed to run all calculations (ground state, AOC, determinants) from one set of fragments, for instance the standard atomic fragments.

content.text:
Benefits of SIC in atomic calculations include (i) improved values for the total energy and for the separate exchange and correlation pieces of it, (ii) accurate binding energies of negative ions, which are wrongly unstable in LSD, (iii) more accurate electron densities, (iv) orbital eigenvalues that closely approximate physical removal energies, including relaxation, and (v) correct long-range behavior of the potential and density, It appears that SIC can also remedy the LSD underestimate of the band gaps in insulators (as shown by numerical calculations for the rare-gas solids and CuCl), and the LSD overestimate of the cohesive energies of transition metals. The LSD spin splitting in atomic Ni and s-d interconfigurational energies of transition elements are almost unchanged by SIC. We also discuss the admissibility of fractional occupation numbers, and present a parametrization of the electron-gas correlation energy at any density, based on the recent results of Ceperley and Alder. .

content.title: Koopmans' condition for density-functional theory
content.text:
This work is organized as follows. First, we reexamine the Perdew-Zunger one-electron self-interaction correction in terms of total and differential ionization energies. Then, after deriving an exact measure of the unphysical curvature of $E_N$ as a function of N based on the generalized Koopmans' theorem, we introduce a functional that minimizes self-interaction errors by enforcing Koopmans' condition, thereby largely eliminating the discrepancy between total and differential ionization energies while restoring the piecewise linearity of the ground-state energy $E_N$ as a function of the number of electrons N. We conclude the study with extensive atomic and molecular calculations to demonstrate the predictive power of the non-Koopmans self-interaction correction.

content.title: Self-interaction correction with Wannier functions
content.text:
# Self-interaction correction with Wannier functions

Massimiliano Stengel<sup>1</sup> and Nicola A. Spaldin<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup>Materials Department, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106-5050, USA (Dated: November 15, 2018)

We describe the behavior of the Perdew-Zunger self-interaction-corrected local density approximation (SIC-LDA) functional when implemented in a plane-wave pseudopotential formalism with Wannier functions. Prototypical semiconductors and wide-bandgap oxides show a large overcorrection of the LDA bandgap. Application to transition-metal oxides and elements with d electrons is hindered by a serious breaking of the spherical symmetry, which appears even in a closed shell free atom. Our results indicate that, when all spherical approximations are lifted, the general applicability of orbital-dependent potentials is very limited and should be reconsidered in favor of rotationally invariant functionals.

#### PACS numbers: 71.15.-m

#### I. INTRODUCTION



In particular, the energy eigenvalue associated with the highest occupied orbital usually shows a strong departure from the ionization potential, while it should match it exactly within exact DFT<sup>6</sup>.

Attempts to correct the self interaction error can be traced back to the seminal paper by Perdew and Zunger (PZ)<sup>7</sup>, who defined the self-interaction corrected (SIC) exchange-correlation energy,  $E_{xc}^{SIC}$ , as

$$E_{xc}^{SIC} = E_{xc}^{\text{approx}}[\rho_{\uparrow}, \rho_{\downarrow}] - \sum_{\alpha\sigma} \left( E_H[\rho_{\alpha\sigma}] + E_{xc}^{\text{approx}}[\rho_{\alpha\sigma}, 0] \right). \tag{2}$$

artificial interaction of electrons with themselves—has been
known for a long time and is still considered a major issue in practical

incorrect wave functions in many kinds of systems, such as artificially
